FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS CALL FOR APPOINTMENT OF FULL-TIME MINISTER-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Federal-provincial co-operative relations have reached a new low resulting in a significant impasse in co-operation and accord between the two levels of government in Canada. The next few years will require intensive federal-provincial discussions, negotiations, co-operation and accord in regard to economic, fiscal, social, legal and constitutional matters. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), with constitutional and other very heavy responsibilities, is overloaded, overworked, near exhaustion, and needs help, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan):
That the Prime Minister immediately appoint a full-time minister of federal-provincial relations with senior cabinet responsibilities to provide continuous and intensive leadership and direction to federal-provincial relations.

Madam Speaker, I believe I have a question of privilege today in that during question period a motivation in certain questions I asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) respecting the so-called John Watkins case was imputed to me by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan).
Over the last few months especially there has been a number of press commentaries relating to statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) regarding ex-ambassador Watkins and by ex-commissioner Kelly of the RCMP on at least one nationally televised program in respect of Mr. Watkins, in several articles which have appeared in national newspapers in this country. I made reference in my questioning to the Prime Minister to one particular set of articles which appeared approximately a week ago in the Toronto Star, a two-part newspaper article, I think, which appeared on a Friday and on a Saturday.
In my reference to these particular articles I said that I had reason to believe-and I reaffirm it before Your Honour and the House here today-that that was an inspired and selected leak from government indicating the part played by the RCMP security service in the unfortunate and perhaps tragic death of ex-ambassador Watkins.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order in regard to matters raised under Standing Order 43 in this House. It has been my understanding, and I seek clarification on this point, that the criteria by which such a motion is measured are whether it is of urgent and pressing necessity, whether or not it is couched in unparliamentary language, or things of that nature. However, I was naturally under the impression, as I am sure all members are, that the Chair, who I am sure will agree with this, is neutral on the merits of the motion. It is up to members of the House to decide after the motion is put whether they consent or not.
Now, Madam Speaker, I would like to ask clarification because today, when I moved a motion under Standing Order 43, if I recall correctly, and I admit I am paraphrasing because the blues are not available as yet, you stated something to the effect that although you could vouch for the fact that the contents contained in my standing order were not accurate, nevertheless you would put the motion. It would seem to me, Madam Speaker, if I am paraphrasing you accurately, that whether or not the House had given its consent is irrelevant. It
means in effect they had been told by the Chair that my motion contains incorrect facts which would mean, therefore, that the House was being influenced on how it should vote.
I would like to seek clarification on whether the Chair is in a position to do that. It seems to me you would not want to be in that position in that the Chair was in effect arguing, as a member opposite might do or as a member on my left might do, that I was wrong and thereby entering into debate with a member. Therefore I am seeking clarification as to why that happened, or just what did happen.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PAYMENTS MADE TO ACTOR AND ACTRESS
subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-MADAM SPEAKER'S COMMENT ON MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Well, I would tell the hon. member that the two of us were wrong. First of all, 1 think the hon. member knows that matters pertaining to the administration of the House which are under the jurisdiction of the Speaker should be dealt with in a different way than matters dealt with in the House precisely because the Speaker cannot enter into debate with any member of the House, or explain or comment on any of the motions put forward by a member. So in this respect I was sort of taken aback by the content of that motion because I knew some of the facts perhaps could be disputed, and I would have preferred to discuss them with the hon. member before entering the House. I think in the future that is the course the hon. member should follow in matters pertaining to the jurisdiction of the Speaker.
Secondly, I was wrong in making that comment and I do apologize to the House. As soon as I made it I realized I was expressing an opinion, something that I should not do. However, the House dealt with the motion in the usual manner. I apologize to the hon. member for my comment but he can follow his own conscience or directive with regard to the fact that he brought these things up in the House when they should have been brought up in another place.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
speechtext:
that Bill S-10, an Act to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Madam Speaker, I rise today for the second reading of Bill S-10, which has already been passed in the Senate.

Bill S-10 is an act to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, known as CALURA. This act, which was originally passed in 1962, provides for the reporting of financial and other information relating to the affairs of corporations and labour unions operating in the country. The information collected under CALURA has been reported annually to Parliament. It has been a valuable and unique reference on the extent and effects of non-resident ownership and control of corporations in Canada, and on the association of Canadians with international labour unions.
During the 18 years the act has been in existence, many changes have taken place in the marketplace. The economy has become much more complex and, as a consequence, policymakers have had to request additional data to keep abreast of developments. The last several years have seen a proliferation of requests for financial data by other government departments which, under the present act, have no access to data of individual corporations collected by CALURA. This has imposed a burden upon respondents, especially smaller enterprises where the resources to cope with this paperwork are severely limited.
[ Translation]
Moreover, since the act covers corporations of a certain size, the number of corporations which must send in a return has greatly increased, even though a great many of them did not originally fall within the purview of the act.
In this time of advanced technology, the administration feels that it urgently needs to keep abreast of technology transfers, even more so since Canada wants to play a role in the ever growing area of technological advances. This need is becoming more acute because of the fact that, more than in any other industrialized economy in the world, corporations in Canada belong to non-residents and are controlled to a large extent by them. In fact, Madam Speaker, there is presently no system which can indicate the level of technological transfers from Canadian corporations to foreign interests or vice versa. Of course, this deficiency will be corrected. With regard to the labour community experience has shown that there are certain deficiencies in the act. Under the terms of the act the defini-

June 17, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions tion of a union has been too restricted, as well as the scope of financial data obtained from international unions.

With these problems in mind, the government has made several attempts over the past three years to bring in appropriate amendments to the act. Generally we have had support from both sides of the House. Our long, consultative process with representatives of business and labour indicated to us that they, too, welcomed these proposed changes. Indeed, the proposed amendments were extensively considered by a committee of the House in 1978. The present bill includes further improvements in response to concerns expressed during those proceedings and in recent deliberations in the other place.
I should like to express my appreciation for the very serious deliberations which took place in the other place and for the co-operation we received from both witnesses and members of the other place.
Time was not on our side in these previous attempts to enact these changes, but I hope the bill will now be disposed of in the House. Therefore I am pleased that Bill S-10, which I believe reflects present-day conditions and will streamline our methods of collecting and disseminating business and labour information, has been introduced early in this session of Parliament and has already received passage in the other place.
The prime objective of Bill S-10 is to alleviate present and potential response burden on many firms reporting to the federal government. The amendments will allow us to eliminate duplication of requests for information and to improve the quality and timeliness of the reports to Parliament. They will enhance the government's understanding of the flow of technology into Canada, supply vital data on the extent of foreign ownership and control, and provide a more comprehensive picture of union activity in the country.

CALURA was passed 18 years ago to collect data, financial and otherwise, concerning corporations and unions operating in Canada. The aim was to report to Parliament and the public on the scope and the effect of the ownership and control by non-residents of corporations in Canada. The act provided that any corporation with assets exceeding $250,000 and/or sales amounting to more than $500,000 must file a return. At that time, these were considered large businesses. Since then, inflation among other things has weakened this definition, and throughout the years, over 90,000 additional corporations have fallen within the purview of the act, most of which were small Canadian-owned businesses which were not originally supposed to be covered by the act. Bill S-10 should dispense more than 70,000 such businesses from having to send in a return pursuant to the act by multiplying by 20 the original threshold for a mandatory return, which was, in fact, completely unrealistic.
Businesses with assets of at least $5 million and with minimum sales of at least $10 million will have to file a return. The bill will also require all corporations with a measure of
foreign ownership to file such a return. In order to avoid any duplication and minimize the number of replies, eight existing questionnaires will be combined into one and the returns will have to be consolidated. Bill S-10 provides that the returns should be filed on a modified calendar year basis, March 31 being the filing date. It will thus be possible to provide consistent information and to table annual reports in Parliament within 12 months following the end of the reference period.
At present, only aggregates of financial data collected under the act are available to users. In many instances, this does not satisfy the needs of government policy departments that require data by individual companies to prepare policy recommendations and analyse their effect. As a result, companies continue to be faced with ever increasing information requests by various government departments.
Bill S-10 proposes to re-establish the conditions which existed prior to the 1965 amendment to CALURA when officials of the federal government had access under the act to financial information provided by individual companies. In this way, the growing needs of policy departments in examining critical economic issues will be met without creating new demands upon business.
However, access to identifiable data for both financial and technology transfers proposed in this bill is more restrictive than it was prior to 1965. First, regulatory agencies, or parts of government departments having regulatory or investigative powers, will be excluded from such access.
Further, this access will be tightly controlled. The information will only be available to analysts for policy purposes upon request of a minister and with the approval of the Chief Statistician who will further specify the manner and conditions of such access. In addition, the bill provides severe penalties to both collector and recipient of such identifiable data in case of disclosure to unauthorized persons. In this way, Mr. Speaker, we are alleviating the concerns of the business community whose views were obtained in discussions earlier.
To improve the government's understanding of the flow of technology from abroad-and this is one of the areas of complete novelty-the bill provides for the collection of selected data on technology transfers. Collection of any data in this area will be preceded, of course, by consultation with business. To alleviate business concern, this bill provides that data to be collected will not include any scientific or technical description of any product or process. It was evident that industry was concerned when it made representations to us that the data which would be collected would not be, in effect, such as to impair in any way commercial or technological information which could be useful to a competitor. Therefore, we have eliminated information of that nature from the reports which must be filed. Returns on such transfers will be made available within the federal government for policy analysis but, as with financial data, this access will be tightly regulated.
June 17, 1981

CALURA has given us considerable insight into the area of foreign ownership and control of companies operating in Canada. For instance, from the 1978 CALURA annual report just tabled, we learn that the top 500 non-financial enterprises in Canada account for 53 per cent of sales, 66 per cent of assets, 66 per cent of profits and 70 per cent of equity. Some 274 of the 500 were foreign controlled corporations.
In addition to ownership information collected under the act, we have produced a highly popular directory entitled Inter-Corporate Ownership, which shows who owns and controls business in Canada. This publication has served executives, market managers, investors, journalists and economists by providing detailed information on the corporate structure of the Canadian economy. Those of us who have paid some attention to the relatively recent publication entitled The Canadian Corporate Elite will see a large number of citations within that publication which are owed to CALURA.
Ownership information collected under CALURA is not confidential and is available to the public through the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In the interests of such public information, Bill S-10 proposes the following improvements: corporations having 50 or fewer shareholders will be required to report to beneficial shareholders. All other reporting corporations may use their share registers to report on shares held. In addition, all corporations will report on options and voting rights held by their directors and the names of any corporations where they have 10 per cent or more of voting rights.
These measures are designed to provide Parliament and the public with accurate and up-to-date information on the ownership and control of corporations. Further, these measures, when integrated with financial information, will achieve a more accurate determination of foreign control and the concentration of corporate power.

Changes affecting labour unions will also lead to significant improvements in the administration of the act, the quality of data and the timeliness of reports. In order to give a more comprehensive image of labour union activity in Canada, the definition of a labour union will be extended to cover any association that has as one of its purposes the regulation of relations between employers and employees. The new definition will include the returns of independent, unaffiliated unions having no premises. In order to give a more comprehensive image of the financial activities of labour unions in Canada, international unions will be required to report all the direct revenues from their Canadian subsidiaries, as well as all expenditures directly related to their Canadian activities. Moreover, financial data pertaining to special funds, such as pension and strike funds, will have to be reported separately from the labour union income and general expenditures. Therefore, actually published financial data will give us a clear picture of the nature of economic and financial activities within labour unions; the quality of the annual report on labour unions will be improved significantly, which will facili-
Corporations and Labour Unions tate the preparation of the comparative analysis provided for in the act.
Further, international unions will be able to file a return, in the form of a note, concerning all the expenditures incurred on behalf of their Canadian members. Such returns will be examined by the CALURA administration with a view to developing an efficient reporting and analysis system for these types of expenditures within two years after the coming into effect of the act. As far as membership is concerned, Bill S-10 will include a number of improvements leading to better information and enhanced usefulness of the data collected. In the first place, unions will be required under the act to submit reports on membership on a calendar year basis. And, finally, data will be immediately made available to federal and provincial departments for the preparation of statistical reports, which will reduce the need for overlapping requests.
Finally, with a view to reducing the time needed to submit the annual report to Parliament, unions will be required to file their returns within 90 days after the year under review. Mr. Speaker, before concluding, I would like to emphasize that Bill S-10 is the outcome of tremendously important studies and discussions. This is an improved bill, reflecting a number of concerns expressed when its predecessor, Bill C-7, was considered by a committee of this House. For instance, the clause providing for a 90-day notice in The Canada Gazette before regulations come into force is another feature of the bill now before us. This measure should reassure to a large extent business and labour, which will now know that consultations will be held on any contentious aspect of the CALURA questionnaire.
As I pointed out earlier, the bill was further improved by an important amendment made in the other place in response to business concerns. It reflects many responsible suggestions expressed along the way. I am confident that Bill S-10 is a sound bill which merits the support of the House.
In conclusion I simply say that we have been well served by an initiative which is now 18 years old but in effect has proved its worth. In Canada we have a particular position, being so close to a major political entity, an economic entity and a union entity, such as the United States. Our correspondence and communications with that country have created specific concerns among Canadians. A large number of these concerns have been alleviated as a result of CALURA in the past, and the substantial improvements we are proposing will improve the system as it exists now.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the soft salesman's tones of the minister responsible for Statistics Canada who has just finished introducing Senate Bill S-10.
This bill is one of the omnibus amendment bills. I was made aware yesterday afternoon, sometime after four o'clock, that it has been selected to become the business of the day. In other words, I guess the House leaders treat these types of bills as Friday bills, and this happens to be a Friday bill which has been inserted on a Wednesday in the hope that it will slip through.
I first became aware of CALURA in the thirtieth Parliament when I was preparing, over a period of nine or ten months, a submission to the Bryce Commission on Corporate Concentration. As most hon. members know, my experience is with small to medium business in Canada and I believe rather strongly that a sense of individualism should survive in the country. Therefore, as I watch us drift closer and closer into a corporate society where we will be collected into larger and larger masses of units, I keep struggling both through my work in the House and with bills, such as this one in the hope that as a result some sense of individualism will survive in our society.
The practice of allowing this type of bill, which is full of amendments, to slip in as a Friday bill in the hope that it will pass through the House in one day and not be noticed, is a very dangerous practice that we are allowing the government to follow. By listening to the minister, as we did today, I came to the conclusion that he really should be a soap salesman. His product is so slippery that it will not even stick to the body. He quietly told us that the bill basically has three parts. It requires corporations to report.
Very lucidly he gave some statistics to show the value of this reporting to society. We have so many corporations in Canada and so many of them are foreign controlled, but never think of thanking foreigners who invest or bring technology to the land. What we want to do today is to punch them out. That seems to be the emphasis.
The minister also told us that the government wants to bring unions under control and it wants to collect information on unions and on union information movements, that is, Canada vis-a-vis the United States. That is all very well and good and I think most of us understand that.
The minister then very quietly introduced the information aspect of the bill. He told us how important it is for us to get some kind of inventory and handle on technological information, intellectual property, trademarks and patents, and so on. If some of us were not aware of what is going on in this country, we might let that slip by us.
I hope the gentlemen behind me on this side of the House will assist me in demanding that there be a full and lengthy debate on the intent of this type of legislation. What we are really dealing with is the beginning of a move to an interventionist, highly structured type of society. We are moving away from the rule of law and away from a respect for property. We have seen that in the constitutional debate. We are moving now into a situation where this is the beginning, the essential element, before the competition act can be brought to this House, when things as important as this are being slipped in through an amending bill which even lawyers cannot read or make any sense out of.
This is an extremely difficult bill. I was belittling myself last night in trying to get through this bill and to understand it. Usually the first thing that happens is that someone over there says, "well, the hon. member hasn't even read the bill." I will put it on the record right now that I have tried to read this bill. I did not understand it. Last night and early this morning I got copies of the Senate debates and Senate committee reports. In all the spare time I had today, I got only that far, but I still have a long way to go. The minister has talked about an important amendment being made in the Senate. With all the deliberation that took place in the Senate, I think the Senate essentially has missed the point and the intent of this bill.
Some members in the other place were suspicious and were asking key questions. However, they did not have the knowledge or the awareness of the grand design and the grand plan which will take us beyond where we are into a highly structured form of government. It is interesting that there is an increasing use of omnibus bills for masses of amendments in which there are some biscuits and cookies, like the minister's little gift, and I believe it was the former president of the Treasury Board who announced it, whereby 50,000 small Canadian corporations will be eliminated from reporting under CALURA.
In the thirtieth Parliament when I was doing work on a view from the street of corporate concentration, what attracted me
June 17, 1981

to CALURA was four or five small businesses in Quebec which had been taken to court and fined under the powers of CALURA. Some of those businesses no longer exist. In fact, I do not know if any of them do. Those little businesses had to pay fines of $700 or $800.
On the other hand, while doing my work on corporate concentration, I found that the holding company for Power Corporation had never filed under CALURA. If Power Corporation or the holding company had been treated in the same manner as these small businesses, which the government likes to talk about protecting and reducing the burden on so much, the holding company for Power Corporation would have been subject to fines of over $3 million. However, they were not taken to court.
CALURA has been on my mind for some time. It is an important piece of legislation that has not been attended to for some time and that needs amending.
Since coming here I have developed a very suspicious nature and my whole personality has changed, but never did I realize that under the guise of Statistics Canada would information be collected which would be the trigger and the key to the sections of the new competition act and competition policy pertaining to intellectual properties and patents. Until this act is passed, the government cannot move to the second phase of their structured society, and bring in the competition act for full and meaningful debate.
As I stand here today, I could speak fast, in emotional, excited terms and conclude in 20, 30, 40 or 50 minutes. However, I am going to take my time because I do not want this bill to be given second reading until members have been awakened to what we are dealing with within this very confused type of legalese.
I find it offensive that more and more often notification of this kind of legislation comes to us late the previous afternoon and is given low priority by the government House leader. He slips it in hoping it will pass. I do not think this bill should pass until members are aware, and use the opportunity to debate the intent of this bill, of just what is going on in this country.
Basically I will direct my remarks to the information sector of the bill because that is where my concern lies. I am reminded by this type of technique of the omnibus bill on metric measurement being slipped through the House back in 1976. Members became emotionally tied up in hectares and tonnes of grain because of all the emotionalism and populism that existed on that subject. There was a sentence in one clause that not one single member of the opposition understood. However, when we started to study metric some two years ago, we found that that clause made Canadian standard measurement illegal.
That is what is going on with legislation in this House. As members, particularly of the opposition, we should stand on guard to expose this type of practice. We should make sure we do not let innocuous sentences, or anything covered with the minister's soft soap, slip by. The hon. member for York-Peel
Corporations and Labour Unions
(Mr. Stevens) advised Your Honour that he will be speaking on this bill. I hope other members will do so as well.
What we are dealing with in terms of type and style is a structured society, which is the whole thrust and design of the present Liberal government and has been for many years. It is a behaviourist type of society where laws are designed to restrict rights, where people are expected to be involved in widely diverse activities and live under the rule of law, and where respect for the rule of law is absolutely essential. They can work within the laws of the land with a degree of freedom, without arbitrary acts and decisions by bureaucrats interfering with that freedom and the desire to be free, energetic and to create wealth.
For the past 15 years we have seen a slow, steady deterioration of that aspect of life in Canada which I was brought up to respect and revere. It was full of faults and flaws, but it evolved from and came out of the Magna Carta. We in Canada are grateful for our freedom. It is the one system that has enabled men living through the ages under a type of parliamentary system to survive the forces of change and still remain free.
As the government moves away from the rule of law and into structure, which this bill starts to do, it loads the breech, putting in the pellets. In my opinion, by doing that, however sincerely, we begin to threaten the very foundation of our freedom.
There are strong moves taking place. Canada has become the laboratory for centralized power and centralized government. We are trying to remove and negate the checks and balances that are at the second level of government in the country, the provincial level. For some of us it is very worrying, even frightening.
The United States has survived because it has had checks and balances built into its system between its federal and state levels of government. I cry out when I see the checks and balances in this country being interfered with, as they are through the constitutional debate and under the guise of a bill of rights in which we are all interested. To me, a bill of rights is protection for minorities and individuals against arbitrary acts on the part of government. That is where it should stop. When we go beyond that, we start to say what our rights are and we start to wipe the blackboard of our common law heritage.
I should like to make it known now as I make my comments at the start of this debate, that I believe in a behavioural type of society. The problem the government is trying to address with its competition law, with its inventory on patents, trade marks, copyrights and all that is contained in Bill S-10, would be unnecessary if we had a strong anti-trust law. Those who stepped outside that strong anti-trust law would be clobbered. In the United States there is a fear of stepping outside their anti-trust laws. The multinational corporations and the large mass of corporations that have almost as much power as the government are terrified of it. That is the way it should be. That is the only way to handle that class of power.

June 17, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
What we have here is an inventory of the owners of all the rights. They are extremely interested in all the intellectual property rights that are transferred to Canada. They are not limiting themselves or dealing with the intellectual property rights and areas of only the multinationals and foreigners. They want all the private owners of these rights registered and in their fdes as well. I wonder if we have figured out what is coming down the pipe next? Some of us might be labelled as being very suspicious. I can see, without having to be too intelligent, and I have never posed as that, that we are delivering ourselves at a hell of a rate as we are now going with the Constitution, acting on that, with the attack on property rights within the Constitution, with the national energy policy, which is confiscation, although they say it is Canadianization, which is hogwash.
You can Canadianize in Canada with fiscal policy, to which the people react. All that we talk about having happened can be done with fiscal policy, which allows the people to work, create and have a little more of the results of their sweat for themselves. We put in laws that have made it almost impossible for those few people in Canada who are capable of managing and co-ordinating all the aspects and factors of business life for the creation of jobs and payrolls to continue, and we have done this with high interest rates and the 83-cent dollar. Perhaps that darn thing should be down around 75 cents. It only benefits the resource industry and makes more and more draw and pull out of the wage packet. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that managers and owners of small and medium business enterprises today are working for paper pushers, working for the government, working for landlords, scratching and trying to keep a balance sheet solid, working for payrolls and getting no thanks at all. Labour laws make it almost impossible to remove people who will not pull their fair share of the load. No wonder more and more people who have tried to dedicate a good part of their life to the public service are having to return into that sector in order to handle the pressures there are today.
It would be blind and foolish of me to say these pressures do not exist throughout the world and throughout different western societies, but these pressures are caused by governments which want to distribute more wealth than the system can create. We have gone beyond the point of no return. Sooner or later, somehow, we must have a corrective reaction, but it does not have to be a bust.
The government provides no leadership at all in warning the people or in delivering to them an industrial strategy or plan that will let us understand the problems of human nature within a free society. Therein lies the problem. We all want more than we are prepared to give or to put in. The socialists, with envy-I guess it is envy-continually attack those people who were born, educated or put into circumstances whereby they could put a combination of education and fact together into the bloodstream, risking savings, taking a chance, creating jobs. All of that is static in Canada.
As I have watched the last ten years in Canada, I have almost cried, because every single major project we have has now been put on hold or on stop, and has been attacked by our NDP friends to the left. Every single major project that could create jobs in Quebec, the Atlantic provinces, across the prairies and in B.C., including new transportation systems with new trucks, new steel, new pipes, new communities, new pumping stations and new taxes; every single one of these projects today which could relieve the billion dollars of draw in unemployment insurance on the federal treasury has been stopped or placed on hold. What a tragedy.
We have had two days of debate on North-South relations. There is a great world debate about how much progress the world can stand, for the injustice of progress is that the first world, the western world, the second world and the communist world depend completely on progress, on growth in gross national product for the well-being of their citizens and for the sustenance of the anticipated levels within those respective societies, so 20 per cent of the world's people are drawing and calling on 85 per cent of the world's resources.
Canada is playing a game. We cannot settle our problems internally, we cannot get an industrial strategy that has any forward planning, but we are drawing non-renewable fossilized resources from the other world. These resources could be available to the Third World because we are capable of providing our own energy internally. The greatest single donation we could make to the Third World-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I simply want to advise the hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), that this bill is to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, and that act is to provide for the reporting of financial and other statistics relating to the affairs of corporations and labour unions carrying on activities in Canada. subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am the first speaker to reply to the government. I have stated that I am offended by the government trying to sneak this bill through-an omnibus amended bill-an issue as serious and as important as the control and inventory of intellectual property, and that is what this bill is doing. If the minister does not understand that, instead of getting up on his feet maybe he should sit around and listen. He acknowledged and thanked members of the other place for all their work. I have told the minister that they missed the essential issue. Perhaps the minister does not understand the game plan. Maybe if he listened, he would understand. I am not going to rush through and deliver this all in 40 minutes, so he has a bit of listening to do.
I was saying, and all this relates to what I am going to say, that we in Canada can make the largest single donation possible to the Third World by getting our act together at home and withdrawing our demand on the Third World for
June 17, 1981

non-renewable fossilized resources. We are totally capable of doing that internally, except for the fact that the process of doing that is caught up in this revolution, in this structured and interventionist society which this incumbent government is now trying to design and impose on us. This started with the constitutional debate, and the other big hammer was the national energy policy. Now we are starting to get into the nitty-gritty, the sleazy, sticky stuff, sold by the softsoap salesman who just finished introducing the bill. We have a trademark package, right on the line. We have Bill S-10 before us in the House now presented as a private bill so it can slip through so nobody will notice it, and right behind it comes the competition bill.
It is interesting to look at the competition bill and the memoranda which have been leaked out and slipped out. Some major changes have been made in the draft of the competition bill. But they are not going to follow the behaviourist pattern of which I have acknowledged I am in favour, in that we should have strong anti-trust legislation, and we should clobber anyone who does not abide by that legislation. Rather than that principle-and this is the philosophical, political debate which is going on, and that is why the minister does not understand what I am saying-what we are now doing is moving into the grand design, the plan for structure and intervention not only in the multinationals, not only in the large corporations, but also in business of the private owners of intellectual property. What is interesting is that in spite of all the additions, changes, amendments and redrafting of other aspects of the bill, the patents clause in the competition bill is pretty well taken verbatim from Bill C-13, so there has been no change in that area.
Here we are with Bill S-10 as the key to the delivery of the competition bill into the House, and a major thrust of that strategy is going to be in intellectual property. I link that back to the debate on property in the constitutional debate because what they are after in that debate is corporate property and intellectual property.
It is interesting that Bill S-10 comes right in after we have had two days of debate on North-South relationships because the North-South question is very much involved in this whole issue. And here comes Bill S-10 right in behind it.
I remind hon. members of a speech I gave some time ago. I will not repeat it, but I referred in a speech in this Parliament to what I consider to be a very important paper, namely, "The Fate of Empires," by Sir John Glubb. This was originally published in Blackwood magazine in November, 1934, volume 320, and in December, 1976, permission was given to the Canadian Law Society Gazette to reprint it. Sir John Glubb gave us a very interesting analysis of the rise and fall of societies and civilizations from the year 800 B.C. all the way through to the present time. He related the problems of human nature in societies, connected up some ten civilizations and said that these stages of the rise and fall of great nations seemed to be the age of pioneers, that is, the outburst of the
Corporations and Labour Unions
nation when people are pioneering and not heavily in demand of material goods. They are pretty close to the basics of life, and they have that dream and future ahead of them. It is an outburst. That is where the vitality and strength of new nations start. Then there is the age of conquests and the age of commerce, and we have seen all that through Europe. We just have to go back through some ten civilizations to follow this.
Then there is the age of affluence. That is where our trouble starts. That is where the rot of human nature starts in social man. From the age of affluence Sir John Glubb identifies the age of intellect. I wanted to raise that because the designers of the strategy I am putting before the House right now are intellectuals. They are very bright men. They have not wasted their time. They were gifted with good minds and good memories. They studied hard, and they have acquired senior positions in the bureaucracy of this democracy.
We go through the age of intellect in all of these ten civilizations, and then we come to the age of decadence. In each of those ten civilizations, intellect preceded decadence. Then Sir John Glubb went on to say what decadence is marked by and so forth. I put that on the record and into this speech because what we are dealing with is the design of intellects.
We have passed through the age of intellects in Canada- we are still dealing with it-and we are well advanced in this society into the age of decadence. We do not learn from history. Someone said that if we do not learn from history, we are bound to repeat the mistakes of the past. I would like to see some of the intellects and some of the brains in this House in all parties apply themselves to the problem of human nature so that we do not have to continue to move into a highly structured interventionist society of which this Bill S-10 represents the pellets in the gun.
There is a linkage. I have talked about the inventory of information which will be demanded. It is a non-voluntary inventory of information. It is going to be mandatory. In the future, after the competition bill is passed that information will be facing foreclosure if it does not meet certain demands. It will be facing revocation because the writings are all in the background literature to all this. It is in aid of Third World countries, and believe me, we have to assist them, but how far do we go in our assistance without having the economic community of the land aware of what the game plan is? That is why I am on my feet taking some time to make a few points here today.
There is a linkage between all of this legislation. There will be Bill S-10 and the information aspects of the CALURA bill. There will be inventory and control. Once they have that, they know where they are, and they have the inventory for the next phase in the competition bill, but there is another bill which is linked with this too, and it relates to FIRA. Mr. Speaker, I know you do not have to read as much as some of us because of your new duties, but you will have to be aware that the FIRA bill is under revision as well, and the drafters of that bill will be linking up Bill S-10, the proposed competition act, FIRA and the new patent law. They are all interrelated. This

I do not know whether as a member I can do anything about it, other than to use my privilege here in the House to stand and make my colleagues aware of what is happening, but I do not want to live under a structured society.

shareholders or partners to go out and risk money in the hope of putting together an economic unit that will have staying power. Well, Mr. Speaker, the problem there is-and again minds like the hon. member opposite will not let a thread of light or knowledge into their heads because only the big guys, the big corporations, the multinationals burying earnings in overhead for their own benefit can afford the staff, the lobbying and the time necessary to deal with the bureaucrats behind the scene-

speechtext: The member is blinded by ambition.

speechtext:
That is a serious issue today. I asked a question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday but 1 was a little too long in the supplementary and Madam Speaker did not allow me to finish, but on that very issue, Mr. Speaker-I hope it is not my wetness, sir, that is causing you all the trouble in the chair. The hon. member opposite might just think about the contents of that editorial. I am using my time here, Mr. Speaker, to reiterate my concern for the threat to my freedom and liberty and that of the people 1 represent when we allow a structuralist and interventionist motivation and thrust by this government to deliver that arbitrary, come-cap-in-hand, yea or nay situation in our lives. That just brings more and more control over individuals. I know full well, because I am standing here saying these things and have said other things in the past, and have the courage to do so if I might say, Mr. Speaker, I know that I cannot go and get a grant, a privilege or a tax credit because I am a bad boy. We are delivering ourselves to a controlled and structured society and it is time members of this House woke up to that fact. It is time the public out there woke up to that fact. Bills like S-10, with their amendment confusion and their omnibus nature, are intended to hide the type of activity that is carried therein.
They come out and tell us that 70,000 small businesses will not have to report, that we have removed this paper burden. It seems to me that the hon. member for York-Peel said that at the last election, and here we are recycling it. We have moved the threshold, as of course we should, from $250,000 in assets or $500,000 in sales, up to $5 million in assets and $10 million in sales. We have relieved 70,000 corporations from reporting under the act, and that is the big headline, the big issue that the minister shovels out into this House.
However, underneath that camouflage is this other cynicism. I repeat, I am aware that the section requiring reporting of technology transfers into Canada will open up a whole new can of worms. If the minister thinks he is going to have a good
June 17, 1981

time with this, I sincerely hope he is mistaken because I can see that what was missed in the committee proceedings of the other place is being opened up now. I think it is a very sleazy game they are playing.
What they are in fact doing is trying to copy an act already in place in Mexico. I also assume they have had a good strong look at Japan. I think the minister mentioned that in his speech. What Japan does is to take another tack. They want to have an inventory, a register of the intellectual property going in and out of that country. But boy, they are tough. If they are going to receive property and manufacture it, they are going to demand that their manufacture be sold in other markets. I do not see this bunch of great industrialists and businessmen over there ever having the guts to do that. I did not see any trade-offs with Japan in terms of the infrastructure required for northeast coal. I will be one that will support an initiative to trade-off Candu reactors in Japan for the availability of a non-renewable resource like northeast coal, one of the most valuable coal beds in the world. Why should we be selling off our resources when we do not have the maximum value added?
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that you can electrify the city of Vancouver with the exothermic reaction from the coking process? Do you know that coke is worth about twice as much as coal in raw form? We do not want necessarily the coking process because it affects our environment and we have those concerns, so we make these kinds of trade-offs. However, do we really sit down with an industrial strategy and deliver intelligent, forward looking, strong trade-offs when we are dealing with the selling out of our resources? In our greed and selfishness we want it all today and we do not give a tinker's darn about our kids tomorrow.
I have been waiting for this industrial strategy of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) because, boy, if it does not have the guts that this country deserves-he has been talking about it forever. He is the guy who was going to resign, Mr. Speaker-or have you forgotten-when interest rates went up to 14 per cent.
Maybe while I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, we should talk about that a little. The structural need in Canada today should not be patterned on the needs of the United States. The history of our needs and growth is different to that of the United States. Why do we not have a debate in this House on what would happen if we lowered interest rates and let the dollar fall? Why not have a standing committee sitting continuously with a hammer and tong draw on all the debate of the economists and others not so formally trained in this country? We cannot continue to go the monetarist route and survive with any semblance of freedom under the rule of law.

them? Do they use them? The answer is no. They talk about an industrial strategy. Where is it?

Why are they delaying that issue, with interests rates running at 21 per cent to 22 per cent and the dollar at 83 cents? Have we debated in the House what a 75-cent dollar would do for awhile? Would it bring down interest rates four or five percentage points? Who would benefit? Who would make windfall profits to offset the other costs? They are drowning initiatives and they are drowning individuals in preparation for a structuralist, interventionist society.
There is a great deal of sincerity in the New Democratic Party. I can relate to much of what members of that party do, but when they continually raise their concern for the small businessman, I become concerned. Will their concerns help us to get to the issue upon which the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism is sitting or perhaps sleeping? Will their concerns help us deal with the issues of interest rates and the value of the dollar? We are playing political games with each other and we all know it. We do not do a service to Canadian constituents at large. We are all working away at narrow political points. It is beyond me. Perhaps we require a debate on how to fill the coffers of an international reserve fund which will stabilize the pressure on the dollar and give us a chance, with a sound industrial strategy, to get back on track. We have ten years of hard, disciplined work to do if we are to avoid a collapse of the system. The hour is upon us. It behooves us all to become involved in the issue, but the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism is sleeping on one of the most valuable and perhaps one of the most important studies to the small and medium enterprise sector. Their priorities are so screwed up it is unbelievable. It discredits the whole system.
I read the speech of the hon. minister on Bill S-10. I understand some of the advantages he described, but I want those points made clear in committee. I want some of the intellectuals behind the drafting of this pyramid of bills, this interconnected triangle of bills and legislation, in committee. I want some of the intellectuals from the community at large to assist hon. members of both opposition parties in preparing debate and questions for those intellectuals. This is where the system fails miserably.
The biggest problem in Canada is the structure of Parliament. We have lost complete control over the power of supply. Our committees system and structure will not let us work on any continuity of thought. We do not have a secretariat behind our committees to match the expertise of the bureaucrats. Therein lies one of our biggest flaws. This is what we should be addressing first. The constitutional issue is not doing that. We are not throughout any of the constitutional debate addressing regionalism, which is the biggest, single, most serious problem in Canada. There is regionalism in metropolitan areas, in provinces and at large in the land. This structure fails to address and link up the regionalism. It wants to destroy regionalism through a central unitary state and it will not work.
I am taking this time because I feel the great debate in Canada can be resolved with an industrial strategy. It can be resolved under the behaviourist philosophy wherein we design laws which tell people what they can do. If they do not obey, we must have the courage and guts to enforce it. If we are to do that, we must address the needed legislation to improve the respect for the rule of law in Canada.
In closing, I should like to talk about the research and development policy.

That is correct, there is not one. For years we have listened to all corners of the private sector tell us what we need in the way of research and development. Basically we need an incentive in our fiscal policy which will allow the entrepreneurs in the boardrooms of the nation to make decisions and to invest high-risk money in unknown areas and in unknown frontiers of technology, on the chance that there will be a reward down the road.
To offset that decision risk, all they ask for is a 25 per cent credit; in other words, 125 per cent of cost. There is no sense doing this for multinational organizations which are already spending millions of dollars of research money, but we could give them an incentive to increase their activity. We could give them the 125 per cent rate on incremental increases over their respective bases. But no, all energy and talent at large in the land is frustrated. They must come cap-in-hand with polished shoes, make appointments, wait in waiting rooms for some civil servant to process an application. Then they must lobby the whole system, and as the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism knows, the small and medium-sized business sector do not have the time, nor can they afford it, for their businesses would go bankrupt.
Give R and D a chance. Give the brains and talent outside the government in this country a chance to prove that they can get it going. Our dilemma today started with the Benson tax legislation of 1971. That is when we started to move into the interventionist society. That is when our bureaucracy started to build. That is when incentives ceased in any savings process in Canada, other than turning every single Canadian who puts his money into a tax shelter into a future debtor of the state. That is what we have done. We have locked up all our savings in pension funds and RRSP funds and none of it is available to the world of work where the need for that dormant capital exists. The rewards are no longer available in Canada for the managers. The rewards are there for the paper pushers, the landowners and the absentee capitalists, not for the talent which can create jobs and add to the value of goods and services.
I would urge all members to read the editorial which appeared in The Globe and Mail today. It deals with the curse of intervention. We have been hearing this for five, six, seven, or ten years and the government will not allow a glimmer of light into its mind. I stand here and say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the path along which it is leading us will turn out to be one of the most tragic eras in Canadian history. We alone in the western world, the western industrialized nations, have the opportunity to be energy self-sufficient. We have the opportunity to put in place massive transportation systems in the form of pipelines. We have the opportunity to electrify railroads across the mountains and the west; and all that diesel fuel which is consumed by those railroad locomotives can be put back into the bank. All we have to do is give the railroads a tax incentive to convert from a non-renewable fossilized source of energy to a renewable electrical source of energy-I think 150 per cent would have done it. We would have had all of that in the bank. That is where the activity is.
The Cold Lake plant has been backed up, as has the new tar sands plant, as has the transportation system, and as have the pipelines for the flow of energy from the Arctic downward. We
June 17, 1981

will be in trouble with a small pipeline to get the oil from the Mackenzie delta down south. We have sent missionaries out into the field who have created activists in all of the outlying communities. And where a strong centralized state is wanted the government has worked harder to create a fractured state, particularly in the north. All of that was ours.
We were one of the few western nations which really could sustain a 5 per cent or 6 per cent growth in our gross national product without a draw on the Third World. We are one of the few countries in the western world with that gift of nature- and we throw it away. What will this government do when the national energy policy is finally settled? It will release the reins on two, three or four megaprojects. We will not have the skills, the trade, the labour, the steel, the transportation, or the people who are used to working. We will create shortages which will compound strikes. We will just drive up the price of everything. We will never have a secondary manufacturing operation in place with that kind of an industrial strategy.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said that he would resign if interest rates went above 14 per cent while he was a member of any government in power. He is still sitting in the House and interest rates are at 21 per cent. He has talked about an industrial strategy ever since I have known him. Now is the time for an industrial strategy. Where is it? Instead of an industrial strategy this government would rather bootleg in bills like Bill S-10, which are a direct attack on intellectual property and on the future freedom of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker,

I have quoted the motion since it appeared to me the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) was speaking about everything but the bill before us. When he did refer to it he referred to it in a negative way. subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
speechtext: I was not speaking against his bill, I was speaking against the changes in this one.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
speechtext:
As the New Democratic Party critic for labour relations I intend to limit my remarks to those aspects of the bill concerning trade unions. I am sure that other members from my party will quite adequately cover the provisions respecting corporations. My only comment regarding that portion of the bill would be that if CALURA has been as bad at reporting the true financial relationship between Canadian branches of U.S. companies and their parent firms as it has been in reporting the true financial picture respecting international unions, then we are probably completely foolhardy to base any of our economic forecasting or policies on those figures.
I am in a very difficult position in debating this bill. We in the New Democratic Party opposed CALURA from day one because we felt it was structurally designed to present an untrue picture of the way in which international unions operate in Canada. We knew from the first day that the figures from CALURA would be used by those people who would like to destroy the trade union movement in Canada. We knew that because the legislation was designed seriously to overestimate the amount of money leaving Canada while at the same time seriously underestimate the amount of money coming into the country, it would be used as a weapon against organized labour in this country.
My dilemma over the bill which is before us today is very simple. This bill contains provisions which will change

June 17, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
CALURA from being a very bad law into just a bad law. If we oppose these amendments then we are put into the position of supporting CALURA as it presently exists, which is completely untenable. However, if we support these amendments, which are only a series of poorly designed half-measures, we will be giving the new legislation credibility which it does not deserve. We will also be voting seriously to increase the workload on volunteer trade union members. Volunteer trade union members have a lot of work on their hands with regard to reporting transfers of membership throughout the various areas. But the reporting provisions in this bill will require that more information be tabled in less time.
We heard the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) ask a question of the minister regarding corporations and the workload they may have. I, too, want to ask that question regarding volunteer people in the many trade unions across Canada, in international trade unions, such as the railway workers. Volunteer people in the unions are not only trying to keep up with the secretarial work and the treasurer's work and the movement of memberships from one place to another, but they will now be requested to get their information into headquarters.
What we on this side of the House would like to see is not a debate over wallpaper amendments, but rather a debate on CALURA itself. We in the New Democratic Party do not oppose the principle that the true financial picture of trade unions should be publicly available. We would be as distressed as any group in this chamber to learn that union dues collected in Canada were being diverted outside of the country. We feel that Canadians have a right to know how their trade union dues are being spent, just as we feel that Canadians have a right to know how their tax dollars are being spent or how the income generated by companies operating in Canada is being spent. But we are not prepared to support a law which only tells half the story, a law which exaggerates how much money is collected and does not even bother to concern itself with how that money is used.
We also feel very strongly about the autonomy of trade unions in Canada. We have always supported the notion that Canadian workers should be in complete control of their own affairs, that Canadian workers should be able to decide how their union operates. But we reject the very simplistic notion implicit in CALURA that the level of Canadian autonomy in a union is a direct function of how many of its dollars are kept in a bank in Canada, as opposed to a bank somewhere else in the world.
Imagine if we used that very simplistic idea in determining the Canadian level of ownership in a company. Instead of concerning ourselves with how that company makes decisions, with how its board of directors is composed, or with what percentage of its stocks were owned by Canadians, imagine basing our decision on what constitutes a Canadian company solely on the basis of where it invested its earnings.
Would the CPR, which has holdings all over the world, then be viewed as a foreign firm? Would Imperial Oil of Canada, which operates exclusively in Canada, then be viewed as a
Canadian firm? That sounds silly, but that is exactly the logic behind CALURA. We would be saying to the trade unions: "We don't care who makes your decisions, we don't care whether you are controlled by your membership, we don't care whether you are democratic, we don't care whether you have complete autonomy; we just care whether or not you happen to keep some of your money in a bank outside of Canada".
Of course, that is not what any of us would say. But that is not to say that we in the New Democratic Party are not concerned with where the money is kept. Speaking quite frankly, we would like to see as much of that money as possible staying in Canada. We would like to see Canadian pension funds invested in Canada. We would like to see Canadian dues and strike funds invested in Canada so that Canadian workers can borrow that money.
Those are concerns, but those concerns are not our greatest ones. We are most concerned that Canadian unions have the full protection they need to fight the sometimes terrible struggles with which they are confronted. We recognize that when Canadian autoworkers, for instance, are fighting Ford, or General Motors, or Chrysler, they need tremendous financial resources to win those battles. When Canadian workers are fighting the huge multinationals which dominate our economy, they need some pretty huge pools of money. The unfortunate reality is that there are not enough union dues in all of Canada to win some of these battles. That is when we recognize the necessity for international ties between workers.
I often wonder about the position of other parties in this chamber on this question. If I were slightly more cynical, I might feel that other parties here are not really interested in keeping our trade union movement strong. I might conclude that they would be most happy to see a small Canadian union fighting some huge American company. Those people who say that our trade union movement should be completely Canadian, that we should break all links with international unions, fall into two camps. A very small percentage of them are truly concerned with what they feel is foreign domination of our union movement. They are usually not acquainted with the facts. They do not know that Canadian trade unions, for the most part, are completely independent: that they elect their own leadership and make their own decisions. But the rest of the people who would like to break up the international unions have a hidden agenda. They know that in many industries the international union is the only salvation for Canadian workers. They know that when General Motors is bargaining in Canada they are bargaining with an international union with over one million members, not with a Canadian union that barely has 10 per cent of that number.
We in the New Democratic Party will be moving many amendments to this bill when it gets to committee. Frankly, we do not understand why on the one hand the law is going to require unions to file a report on their income, but on the other hand there is only a request that they file their expenditures in Canada. We want the law to require international unions to spell out in very clear language how their money is spent in Canada. We want them to itemize such things as the Canadian
June 17, 1981

share of the costs in running the international headquarters. We want them to itemize the Canadian share of the cost on the depreciation of fixed assets. If they do that, then maybe we will get a true picture of exactly how much money is either flowing into Canada or, in some rare cases, flowing out of Canada.
Finally, we are concerned about the impact that all these extra forms will have on the volunteer staff who must fill them out at the local level. I have often heard my friends to the right complaining about the paper burden which many small businessmen face when having to fill out government forms. I sympathize with those concerns, but I would suggest that in this case the burden is even more overwhelming, since in many cases the forms must be filled out by elected officials at the local level in their own time. I would like to see these officials remunerated in some way for work which they will be doing on behalf of the government.
In conclusion, let me just repeat what 1 said earlier. We in the NDP favour a law which will provide for the fair and accurate reporting of money spent in Canada and of money collected in Canada by the trade union movement. The present law does not come close to doing that. The amendments are an improvement, but even if they are passed in their present form, CALURA will not be providing a fair or an accurate assessment of how unions operate in Canada.

The government wants to try in this country what has failed so dreadfully in Sweden and England and is in trouble in Russia. Why does the government impose this on us, taking away our freedoms and our rights?
The government keeps on spending money. That is the politically acceptable thing to do. It is now at the point where it is borrowing capital funds from foreign sources in order to meet its social objectives. Those objectives are important. But when this erodes the private sector of this country, it erodes the entire economy.
This government does not care about the private sector. It wants to get its hands on it. It wants to intrude upon it and erode it. I referred to other countries which tried this. It is too late for her, but I do not believe it is too late for the United States. That country is fortunate in having a leader who is communicating with the people, not telling them untruths. He is again giving them a spirit of freedom. The Americans are in the fortunate position that their private sector has not been eroded. They have the opportunity to bring that country back to the original system they were working under.
I cannot say that we should accept any other model. Our country is different. It is half a continent spread over 3,000 miles. It is not a cohesive country for geographic and regional reasons. It is not like France which has Paris as a hub around which its economy revolves. It is not like half of Germany with its hub around Berlin. It cannot be treated like England with its hub around London. The proximity and the thinking of the people is so close to those centres that they can communicate the common purpose. In this country it is different. We have different cultures, different languages and a much more serious problem which this government is not addressing. With its mandate, it has an opportunity to develop an economic system that would be unique to Canada. It must be unique to Canada because we are different from other countries.
The previous speaker talked about the inventory of rights. Our inventory is slowly eroding and washing away. The government is slowly but surely taking it or pushing it away. Look what it is doing with the National Energy Program, Bill C-48 and Bill C-57. It is forcing the wealth out of this country or underground and removing the funds from the private sector. This government should do an analysis to determine the total

I referred before to the potential confiscation that exists in this measure, particularly when it is tied to Bill C-48 and its confiscation of 25 per cent of the rights of oil companies. This frightens me. I just wonder why we are here. I wonder why the government is trying to sneak these things through on us. The government brings these things through in saddening ways through different bills; a little bit here, a little bit there, a little bit through the Constitution, a little bit through Bill C-48 and a little bit through Bill C-57.
By Bill C-57 the government is taking away the rights of the provinces. The provinces enjoyed the right of royalty on natural resources. The government is being specific in that regard, but in this measure it is no longer being specific. The government is going to go after all other resources. It will get the statistics and the information. The government will watch growth and will have a chart on each corporation that is

growing. As the corporations grow the government will say: "Aha! The nickel industry is looking good this week; let's go after it". I am very concerned.
We have talked about patent rights, and I guess copyrights could be included. What the government is trying to do through a bill is tax a Canadian corporation which has the intelligence, the aggressiveness and the wherewithal to go out and buy rights from somebody else who has done the development. The reason that development takes place somewhere else is that most countries in the world are very aware of research and development. They provide a very strong incentive to encourage research and development in the private sector. This government figures, why should it subsidize the private sector? It feels it should not have to subsidize the private sector. It will go after the companies that buy these rights and bring them back to Canada. It will nail the companies that way and get patents free. From a private point of view I think this is commendable. These are the kinds of things the private sector does through ingenuity. What this government is doing is beyond ingenuity. We in this country have a responsibility to contribute to research and development. We have a responsibility to help people develop new products. We have a responsibility to help the industrial base modernize and to help labour become more productive. We are doing nothing for them.
Japan and Germany are far ahead of us right now in robotizing the auto industry. General Motors in the United States is moving very quickly now. It is doing the reverse of what Japan did before the war. It is stealing ideas from Japan and perfecting them. Once General Motors perfects robotizing of auto production the government will turn right around and collect all that information here in Canada through Bill S-10. That is a parasitic clause in the bill, together with many of the others.
This bill worries me. As I said before, perhaps some ingenious entrepreneurs will find ways to get around this bill. It will create lots of work for lawyers and accountants, but again it is an indirect tax. This bill is a total erosion of the rights of Canadian citizens who are entrepreneurs. It is very similar to leaving property rights out of the Constitution. It is very similar to taking away royalty rights under Bill C-57. It is just a continuation. Mr. Speaker, I think this bill should be considered in the context of freedom of information. I find it contradictory, strange and ironic that the party to my right, which has so strongly espoused the policy of requiring the government to provide greater information to the public-a policy which we have advocated for a great many years-should now appear to be opposed to the principle of the right of citizens to know the nature and structure of those corporations and the nature and structure of those trade unions which exercise such a substantial degree of power in our society.
I find it quite fantastic to hear the tremendous rage-the sincerity of which I do not question and with which I continue to be impressed-expressed with respect to the nature of the corporate world out there and the nature of the trade union world, which I am quite happy to talk about, and to hear the concerns expressed by members of the Conservative party. I think this is a departure from the historic traditions of that party but, nevertheless, there is a feeling, expressed by a wing of the Conservative party that any requirement with respect to the reporting of critical financial information is an act of impending totalitarianism and simply one more step on the slippery slope toward a totalitarian state.
That position is one which, as I say, has been expressed with a great deal of sincerity. I know it is deeply felt but I just do not think it conforms to the nature of the world in which we live. All I can say is that it is an understandable reaction to the frustration which all of us in the opposition parties feel about the inactivity of the present government with respect to the
economy. It is an understandable frustration which I certainly feel.
When I heard the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) talk about the absence of an industrial strategy and the foolhardiness of the government of British Columbia in deciding to sell off lots of coal very cheaply, I could only say "hear, hear!' It is a position I share. When I hear criticism of the government's high interest rate policy coming from the same member, I agree with him. Unfortunately the person he has to convince is his colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), who just ten days ago defended the high interest rate policy of Governor Bouey and said if he was minister of finance he would be defending it as well.
With respect to what he had to say on those matters, I was in substantial agreement. However, when it comes to looking at the principles involved in legislation of the CALURA type first introduced by the Diefenbaker government in the early 1960s, it seems to me the question is this. In addition to requiring a government to respond to the demands of its citizens, their right to know what is going on in government, the nature of the power being exercised by the government and our rights as citizens to access to critical information with respect to decisions being made, how can one then turn around and say that corporations whose power, even on the admission of the hon. member for Capilano, has grown substantially, who are exercising substantial power over the individual, should be even further increased? I think I heard the hon. member say that in many instances their power rivals that of government. The hon. member for Capilano and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) both made passing references to the power of trade unions which I do not entirely accept. I think they exaggerate the power of the trade unions. Listening to the hon. member for Ontario talking about the billions in assets that international unions have, it demonstrates an ignorance about union finances which is astonishing.
Nevertheless, despite that fact, if you say these groups exercise substantial public power, surely at some point we abandon the mythological notion that we are simply talking about interference with privacy. Some other principles have to be established. At some point those groups have a responsibility to the public to give up information which is of concern and direct interest to the public. I say to the members of the Conservative party, who I know will be participating at great length in this debate and with some interest, that surely the question is not that all of this is on the slippery slope to totalitarianism; surely the question should be: What information do we really want and need to know-
